findings.claim: In the 1960s, Goldthorpe and Lockwood had studied male manual workers at the Vauxhall car plant in Luton, arguing that affluent workers were becoming embourgeoisified
findings.truth: Goldthorpe and Lockwood tested the embourgeoisement thesis and REJECTED it. The Affluent Worker studies found the Luton workers kept a distinct working-class outlook; the researchers proposed privatised instrumentalism and the 'new working class' instead. The lesson credits them with the very thesis they disproved.
findings.evidence: spec 7.4 (Devine entry: she 'tested Lockwood's idea that privatized instrumentalism would become typical' and 'rejected the idea of the new working class'); Wikipedia, Embourgeoisement thesis ('Goldthorpe disputed the embourgeoisement thesis in 1967')

findings.claim: Which sociologist revisited the Luton car plant workers in the early 1990s...
findings.truth: Devine's fieldwork was in the late 1980s; 1992 is the publication year of Affluent Workers Revisited. The lesson body already says 'late 1980s', so the question stem contradicts it.
findings.evidence: spec 7.4: 'During the late 1980s Devine interviewed a sample of male manual workers employed at the Vauxhall car plant in Luton and their wives.'

findings.claim: What did Devine find when she revisited the Luton car workers in the early 1990s?
findings.truth: Same date error as F2: the fieldwork was in the late 1980s.

findings.claim: Weber's three types of authority are all forms of formal power - power that operates through official channels and recognised institutions.
findings.truth: Charismatic authority is defined by Weber as resting on the person, not on an office or rule, so it is not a form of power exercised through official institutions. The spec lists traditional, charismatic, rational-legal, formal and informal as parallel forms, not as a hierarchy with formal power on top. Teaching that all three are formal power would lead a student to classify a charismatic movement leader as formal power.
findings.evidence: spec 3.6.5 ('including traditional, charismatic, rational-legal, formal and informal sources of power'); spec 7.4 Weber entry (charismatic = 'devotion to a leader who has exceptional qualities')

findings.claim: The mark scheme expects: the correct name (1 mark), the source of legitimacy explained (1 mark), and a developed example (1 mark).
findings.truth: An invented mark-scheme breakdown. It also contradicts this lesson's own practice keys, which award 1 mark for naming and 2 for the developed description on the same question type. The spec sets no per-mark descriptors.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section (lines 299-325) gives paper structure only; L5 practice questions 3 and 5 use a 1 + 2 split

findings.claim: Fiona Devine's return to Luton to revisit workers first studied by Goldthorpe and Lockwood is an example of a longitudinal research design
findings.truth: Devine's study is a restudy (replication in the same locality), not a longitudinal design. She interviewed a fresh sample of Vauxhall workers, not the same individuals. The same paragraph correctly defines a longitudinal study as one that tracks the same individuals over time, so the lesson contradicts itself in a methods lesson.
findings.evidence: spec 7.4: 'By returning to Luton she was able to make a direct comparison with the work of Goldthorpe and Lockwood in the 1960s'

findings.claim: It [the Crime Survey for England and Wales] interviews a random sample of around 50,000 households each year
findings.truth: The CSEW achieved sample is about 31,000 adults aged 16+ plus about 1,500 children aged 10-15 each year. The ~50,000 figure has never been the current sample; the old British Crime Survey peaked around 46,000 adults before the 2012 reduction.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Crime Survey for England and Wales: 'around 31,000 people aged 16 or over, and 1,500 children aged 10 to 15 years'

findings.claim: An annual victim survey of around 50,000 households asking whether they have been victims of crime
findings.truth: Same inflated sample size as F7; about 30,000 adults a year.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Crime Survey for England and Wales

findings.claim: Murray identified what he called a dependency culture
findings.truth: Murray's own terms were 'underclass' and welfare dependency; 'dependency culture' is a British New Right phrase that GCSE textbooks routinely attach to him. 'What he called' slightly over-attributes the wording, but the idea is correctly his and the spec describes exactly this argument.
findings.evidence: spec 7.4 Murray entry (underclass, benefit dependency; the phrase 'dependency culture' does not appear)

findings.claim: House-wide pattern: every exam tip in this unit asserts what 'the mark scheme rewards' or 'the mark scheme expects' (L1, L2, L3, L4, L6, L7), and the practice keys carry house band labels (Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging).
findings.truth: Two options. (a) Leave them: none of the surviving claims states anything false - they describe generic requirements of a 'how far would sociologists agree' answer, the band labels are house vocabulary, not AQA wording, and the same pattern runs across roughly 1,289 lesson files platform-wide, so a unit-level rewrite would be inconsistent. (b) Re-voice them platform-wide to 'a secure answer does X' as a separate programme. Only the L5 instance made a specific fabricated claim, and that is fixed as F5.
findings.evidence: grep across scripts/_retrofc/units: 1,289 lesson files use the same band labels
findings.ruling: NOTE: house band labels and 'mark scheme rewards' phrasing left for the programme-wide examiner-voice / band-ladder sweeps.

summary: Seven lessons checked against AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 (3.6 and 3.7 plus the section 7.4 key-thinker entries). One HIGH: lesson 3 credits Goldthorpe and Lockwood with the embourgeoisement thesis they actually tested and rejected. Six MEDIUM fixes cover Devine's fieldwork date, the claim that all three Weberian authority types are formal power, an invented 3-mark breakdown, Devine's restudy mislabelled longitudinal, and an inflated CSEW sample size in two places. All sociologist attributions, dates and numbers otherwise match the spec (Davis and Moore 1945, Townsend 1979 with over 22% in 1968-69 against just over 6% on the state standard, Murray Losing Ground 1984, Walby's six structures and the private-to-public shift, Weber's three authority types); all 35 knowledge-check answer keys are correct.
